_meta.schema: signature: id, pattern (JS regex source, case-insensitive), title, meaning, disease, first_moves[], tree (id into trees.json or null), source, verified

signatures.pattern: Failed to create temporary directory|Authentication or permission failure.*tmp|ansible-tmp-
signatures.title: Remote temp directory failure
signatures.meaning: Ansible could not create or use its working directory (~/.ansible/tmp by default, the remote_tmp setting) on the target while staging a module.
signatures.disease: Module execution stages a payload in a temp dir before running it. Broken home directory, wrong permissions, a full disk, or noexec on the filesystem breaks the staging step. Pipelining can mask this — it bypasses the temp dir, it does not fix it.
first_moves: ssh to the target as the ansible user: can you mkdir -p ~/.ansible/tmp?
df -h — is the home filesystem full?
mount | grep noexec — is home or /tmp mounted noexec?
Check remote_tmp in ansible-config dump --only-changed

signatures.pattern: Missing sudo password|password is required to run sudo|sudo: a password is required
signatures.title: Become needs a password you didn't supply
signatures.meaning: The task escalates with become, the target's sudo wants a password, and none was provided.
signatures.disease: Either run with -K (--ask-become-pass), configure NOPASSWD in sudoers for the automation user (site policy call), or set become_password via vault. Without any of these, runs error out — or hang at an invisible prompt.
first_moves: Re-run with -K
ssh in and run sudo -l as the ansible user to see what sudoers grants
Decide policy: NOPASSWD for the service account, or vaulted become password

signatures.pattern: host key checking is enabled|REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED|authenticity of host .* can't be established
signatures.title: SSH host key not accepted (or changed)
signatures.meaning: SSH refused to connect or wants interactive confirmation of the target's host key.
signatures.disease: First contact needs the key accepted; a CHANGED key means the host was rebuilt — or something is impersonating it. In a batch run the prompt is invisible, so it looks like a hang or an instant failure.
first_moves: ssh to the host manually once and inspect the fingerprint
If the host was legitimately rebuilt: ssh-keygen -R <host> then reconnect
If NOT rebuilt: stop — treat as a security event, verify out-of-band
Fleet policy: pre-populate known_hosts; avoid blanket host_key_checking=False

signatures.pattern: UNREACHABLE!|Failed to connect to the host via ssh|Connection timed out|No route to host
signatures.title: Host unreachable over SSH
signatures.meaning: The transport never came up — Ansible couldn't SSH to the target at all. This is network/SSH-layer, not module-layer.
signatures.disease: Wrong ansible_host, DNS, firewall, sshd down, or the box is off. UNREACHABLE always means 'fix connectivity first, Ansible is fine'.
first_moves: ping <host> and ssh <user>@<host> by hand
ansible-inventory --host <host> — is ansible_host/ansible_port what you think?
On console/OOB: systemctl status sshd; firewall-cmd --list-services includes ssh?

signatures.title: Python interpreter problem on the target
signatures.meaning: The transport worked but the module couldn't run: the Python Ansible tried to use isn't there (or died instantly).
signatures.disease: Modules are Python programs executed on the target. Minimal installs may lack Python, or it lives at a nonstandard path. raw/script modules work without Python — that contrast is the diagnostic tell.
first_moves: ansible <host> -m raw -a 'which python3 || ls /usr/bin/python*'
Set ansible_python_interpreter for the host/group if the path is nonstandard
Truly Python-less target: install it with -m raw, or manage via raw only

signatures.title: Module died mid-execution — several diseases share this symptom
signatures.meaning: The SSH session was up, the module started, and then the connection dropped. This message alone does NOT identify the cause — it accompanies a missing/crashing Python interpreter, an out-of-memory kill, a dying sshd, or a module that segfaulted.
signatures.disease: Ansible reports the transport closing, not why the process on the far end died. The evidence is on the TARGET, not in this message.
first_moves: Probe the interpreter first (cheapest to rule out): ansible <host> -m raw -a 'ls /usr/bin/python*'
On the target: journalctl -p err -b and dmesg | tail — look for OOM-killer or segfault lines around the timestamp
Check sshd health on the target: journalctl -u sshd --since '10 minutes ago'
Re-run the task with -vvv and read the full module traceback if one was captured
signatures.source: ansible error taxonomy, paraphrased — deliberately low-confidence signature

signatures.pattern: Decryption failed|no vault secrets found|Attempting to decrypt but no vault secrets found
signatures.title: Vault password missing or wrong
signatures.meaning: The play references vault-encrypted content and Ansible has no (or the wrong) vault password.
signatures.disease: Encrypted files need their password at runtime: --ask-vault-pass, --vault-password-file, or vault_password_file in ansible.cfg.
first_moves: Re-run with --ask-vault-pass
ansible-vault view <file> to confirm the password works at all
Check vault_password_file path in ansible-config dump --only-changed

signatures.pattern: The task includes an option with an undefined variable|'\w+' is undefined|AnsibleUndefinedVariable
signatures.title: Undefined variable
signatures.meaning: A template or task referenced a variable that has no value for this host.
signatures.disease: The var is misspelled, defined for a different group, or gated behind gather_facts: false (ansible_* facts don't exist if facts weren't gathered). Precedence surprises land here too.
first_moves: ansible-inventory --host <host> | grep -i <var> — does the host actually have it?
Using ansible_* facts? Confirm gather_facts is on for the play
Add a debug: var=<name> task right before the failure
Consider | default('value') where absence is legitimate

signatures.pattern: is not a valid attribute for a (Play|Task|Block)|conflicting action statements|no module\/action detected in task
signatures.title: Playbook structure error — wrong keyword, wrong level
signatures.meaning: YAML parsed fine, but a keyword sits at the wrong level (a task key on a play, two modules in one task, or a module name typo'd so nothing looks like an action).
signatures.disease: Playbook grammar: plays hold hosts/vars/tasks; each task holds exactly one module plus task keywords. Indentation drift moves keys between levels without breaking YAML syntax.
first_moves: Read the reported line: is that key at play level when it belongs to a task (or vice versa)?
Exactly one module per task?
Module name spelled right? ansible-doc <name> to confirm it exists
Run the file through this tool's Gotcha Linter for indent drift

signatures.pattern: could not find expected ':'|mapping values are not allowed in this context|found character '\\t' that cannot start any token|YAML syntax error
signatures.title: Raw YAML syntax error
signatures.meaning: The file isn't valid YAML at all — the parser died before Ansible even looked at it.
signatures.disease: Tabs (YAML forbids them for indentation), a missing space after a colon, or a stray quote. The reported line number is where the parser GAVE UP, which is often one line below the actual mistake.
first_moves: Look at the reported line AND the line above it
Hunt tabs: grep -P '\t' <file>
Paste the file into this tool's Gotcha Linter
ansible-playbook --syntax-check after each fix until clean

signatures.pattern: Permission denied \(publickey|Permission denied, please try again
signatures.title: SSH authentication rejected
signatures.meaning: The target's sshd refused the credentials — wrong user, missing/wrong key, or password auth disabled.
signatures.disease: Ansible connects as ansible_user (or your login name if unset) with the default key. Mismatch between the user you tested by hand and the user Ansible actually uses is the usual gap.
first_moves: ansible-inventory --host <host> — what ansible_user is actually set?
ssh -i <keyfile> <ansible_user>@<host> by hand
On the target: ~<user>/.ssh/authorized_keys present, mode 600, home not group-writable?
Key auth requirements broken? Check sshd_config PubkeyAuthentication and SELinux contexts on .ssh (restorecon -Rv ~/.ssh)

signatures.pattern: you must have a tty to run sudo|sudo: sorry, you must have a tty
signatures.title: sudoers requiretty blocks non-interactive sudo
signatures.meaning: The target's sudoers has requiretty set; Ansible's non-interactive sessions have no TTY, so sudo refuses.
signatures.disease: Legacy hardening default on older RHEL. Fix in sudoers (Defaults:ansible_user !requiretty via a sudoers.d drop-in, validated with visudo -c) — pipelining also conflicts with requiretty, so this often appears right after enabling pipelining.
first_moves: On the target: grep -r requiretty /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d/
Add a drop-in exempting the automation user; validate with visudo -c
Note the interaction: pipelining=true requires requiretty off for the automation user

signatures.title: SELinux denial
signatures.meaning: SELinux blocked an access — the process's context isn't allowed to touch the target's context.
signatures.disease: Usually mislabeled files (moved with mv, created in the wrong place) or a boolean that's off. Almost never a reason to disable SELinux.
first_moves: ausearch -m AVC -ts recent — read the actual denial
Files recently moved/created? restorecon -Rv <path>
getsebool -a | grep <service> — is there a boolean for exactly this?
Only then: audit2why for an explanation

signatures.pattern: No space left on device|Disk quota exceeded
signatures.title: Filesystem full
signatures.meaning: A write failed because the filesystem (or quota) is at 100%.
signatures.disease: Services fail in strange ways when /var or /tmp fills: logs stop, PID files can't write, databases wedge. Note: deleted-but-open files still hold space until the holder restarts.
first_moves: df -hT — which filesystem, exactly?
du -xh <mount> | sort -rh | head -20 — what's eating it?
lsof +L1 — deleted files still held open?
Free space, then restart whatever was wedged

signatures.title: Port already taken
signatures.meaning: A service tried to bind a port that another process holds.
signatures.disease: Two services configured for one port, or a zombie instance survived a bad restart.
first_moves: ss -tulpn | grep :<port> — who has it?
Same service, old PID? systemctl restart it properly
Different service? Decide who moves; check for copy-pasted config

signatures.pattern: Cannot download.*repodata|Failed to download metadata for repo|Errors during downloading metadata
signatures.title: dnf can't reach its repositories
signatures.meaning: Package metadata download failed — repo unreachable or misconfigured.
signatures.disease: On an air-gapped box this means the local mirror path/URL is wrong, the mirror is down, or the repo file changed. Nothing to do with rpm itself.
first_moves: dnf repolist — which repos are configured?
curl the baseurl from the repo file by hand
Air-gapped: is the mirror mounted/served? Correct path in the .repo file?
